chore(packer): pin the builder version, and make CI agree with it (#514-adjacent) (#520)

Every template said `required_version = ">= 1.10"`, so any Packer from 1.10
onward could build the guest images and no artifact recorded which one did. The
builder is an input to the image — a different Packer can produce a different
guest — and that is the same defect as the floating
`mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0` tag that left the dotnet-analysis image
unbuildable once the tag moved under a reusable cache (#514).

Pinned to `~> 1.16.0` in all six templates: patch releases inside 1.16.x stay
allowed so a security fix is not blocked, and a minor bump becomes a decision
rather than a surprise.

packer/README.md records the exact release, its sha256, and the verify-then-
install steps — a constraint says which versions are ALLOWED, but reproducing an
image needs the one that was USED. Installed as a pinned binary rather than from
HashiCorp's apt repo, which tracks latest and would reintroduce the same drift.

The version I first proposed (1.11.2) was stale; the release index says 1.16.0,
2026-07-24. Checked rather than asserted.

CI ALSO DECLARES A PACKER VERSION, and it said `~1.11`. Raising the templates
without moving CI would have made every `packer validate -syntax-only` fail —
a job that cannot pass is not a check. Two places declaring the same thing with
nothing making them agree is the drift this commit is about, so a test now
asserts the CI version and the template constraint share a series.

Still not pinned, and said so in the README rather than left implicit: `packer
init` fetches the qemu plugin (`~> 1.1`) from GitHub. The `.pkr.hcl.lock` file
it writes is the mechanism that fixes that, and should be committed after the
first init.

Mutations: one template drifting back to `>= 1.10` fails two tests; CI drifting
back to `~1.11` fails a third.

Commit `131734f2c007d0009a7fc218849f4ede66c7c899`. Message-only evidence; first parent not required. Message:
manager: reload the services when an environment file changes

A change to netbox_role_mapping never reached the inventory reconciler on a
production manager. The new value was in
/opt/manager/configuration/inventory-reconciler.env, `osism apply manager`
reported changed=0, and the running container still had the mapping it had been
created with, so the generated inventory kept the old host groups and the
symptom was silent: the reconciler completed and wrote every file.

Only the docker-compose.yml template in service.yml notifies a handler. The
eleven tasks that render an environment file notify nothing, so a change to any
manager environment value is written to disk and never delivered to the
container that reads it. The environment of a container is fixed when it is
created, so a restart cannot pick it up either, the container has to be
recreated.

They now notify "Ensure that all containers are up" rather than "Restart
manager service". That handler runs

    docker compose --project-directory /opt/manager up -d

which is exactly what delivers a new environment, and no more. Measured with
docker 29.7.2 and compose v5.5.0 on a two service project:

  * env file changed, then docker restart: same container id, old value
  * env file changed, then compose up -d: new container id, new value
  * compose up -d with nothing changed: same container id, nothing recreated
  * two services, only one env file changed: only that service is recreated

The last two lines are why this handler is the right one. Notifying "Restart
manager service" instead would restart the whole manager stack through systemd
and then wait the hardcoded minute of "Wait for manager service to start" for
every environment change, even though compose narrows the work to the services
whose environment actually differs.

yamllint with the repository configuration and ansible-lint at the production
profile are clean on roles/manager.
